The mediation MR analysis in the current study showed that adjusting for genetic diabetes liability reduced the BMI–mortality association by about 56%, directly supporting the explanation that inclusion of BMI's lifelong effects mediated via diabetes accounts for the larger relative risks observed in the current report.

15.Option: Despite the growing prominence of the interventional framework in epidemiology, most studies that aimed to estimate intervention effects did not specify a 'how' that adhered to consistency, and only a minority of these studies had well-defined interventions.

Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85).
15.Rationale: The passage states that the interventional framing is increasingly adopted, then reports that only 29 studies explicitly stated exposure contrasts as hypothetical interventions. Among those 29, only one study (3%) detailed the 'how' and only 38% (11/29) were judged to have well-defined interventions. These explicit figures directly support the conclusion that despite growing prominence, most intervention-effect studies did not specify a 'how' that adhered to consistency and only a minority had well-defined interventions.

Evidence: Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ).
Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85).

when studies of such exposures simply stated—without justification—that treatment variation irrelevance was assumed (or ignored the assumption entirely), we concluded they had ill-defined interventions.
15.Rationale: The passage documents that almost all intervention-effect studies did not detail a 'how' (only one did), and that some studies were judged to have well-defined interventions only because authors invoked treatment variation irrelevance rather than articulating a 'how'. The authors explicitly note that when studies 'simply stated—without justification—that treatment variation irrelevance was assumed (or ignored the assumption entirely),' those studies were judged ill-defined. Taken together, this supports the inference that studies often implicitly assumed treatment variation irrelevance and that such assumptions were frequently left unjustified in the paper.

Evidence: epidemiological datasets often lack sufficient detail from which to operationalize well-defined interventions (e.g. datasets may contain information on respondents’ duration of physical activity but lack information on activity type).
Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85).

In contrast, no intervention-effect studies of obesity/BMI, substance use, health behaviours, nutrition and/or physical activity had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online).

We concluded a study had a well-defined intervention if: (i) authors specified a ‘how’ that reasonably adhered to consistency, or (ii) when authors did not specify a ‘how’, they cogently argued for treatment variation irrelevance or, more generally, why consistency was likely satisfied or why consistency violations were likely inconsequential.
15.Rationale: While the passage does state that epidemiological datasets 'often lack sufficient detail' (e.g. missing activity type), it does not assert that absence of detailed data is the primary reason for lack of well-defined interventions across most studies. The authors also attribute well-defined interventions to either explicit specification of a 'how' or to cogent arguments for treatment variation irrelevance, and they note that some studies did justify treatment variation irrelevance. The passage therefore identifies multiple reasons (including lack of specification, lack of justification, and data limitations) and does not claim the primary cause is data absence in socio-structural studies. The specific claim that socio-structural factors are chiefly responsible is not supported by the text.

15.Option: The interventional framework's emphasis on specifying a 'how' for interventions enhances the policy relevance of epidemiological findings by enabling predictions about real-world outcomes if the exposure contrast were applied.
Evidence: This framing has several purported advantages. Just 34% (40/117) of non-intervention-effect studies discussed results’ intervention or policy relevance, compared with 59% (17/29) of intervention-effect studies.

Only 41% (12/29) of intervention-effect studies discussed intervention feasibility, and few studies of either type (≤10%) stated predictions about what would happen to outcome burdens if their exposure contrast was applied in the real world.
15.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that a key advantage of the interventional framing is that it 'facilitates predicting the effects of actual interventions, making findings policy relevant.' Empirical findings in the review show intervention-effect studies more frequently discussed policy relevance than non-intervention-effect studies, although few made explicit predictions about outcome burdens. Thus the passage supports the inference that specifying a 'how' enhances policy relevance by enabling predictions about real-world outcomes, even though in practice such predictions were infrequently provided.

15.Option: The majority of studies using g-methods or TMLE failed to meet the consistency assumption because they did not define their exposure in terms of a hypothetical intervention, regardless of data quality.

Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ).
Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85).

Therefore the statement overreaches the evidence in the passage.

Evidence: we found evidence for a nonlinear relationship with tuberculosis risk increasing faster at lower BMI values and decreasing more gradually at higher BMI values, particularly among people with HIV (e.g. coefficient for nonlinear term in the general population = 0.12, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table S3 and Figure 3 ).

In the piecewise linear models, the reduction in tuberculosis risk per one-unit increase in BMI was 18.0% (95% CI: 16.4–19.6) for BMI of <25.0 kg/m2 and 6.9% (95% CI: 4.6–9.2) for BMI of ≥25.0 kg/m2 in 22 general-population cohorts ( n = 24,921,531); 15.3% (95% CI: 13.1–17.5) for BMI of <23.0 kg/m2 and 2.6% (95% CI: –3.1–7.9) for BMI of ≥23.0 kg/m2 in 18 cohorts of people with HIV ( n = 162,609); and 20.5% (95% CI: 18.4–22.6) for BMI of <24.0 kg/m2 and 13.4% (95% CI: 3.9–22.0) for BMI of ≥24.0 kg/m2 in three cohorts of people with diabetes ( n = 1,118,424) ( Figure 3 ).

Evidence: There were also six cohorts of household contacts of people with tuberculosis (three in Peru, two in India, and one in Southern Africa) [ 27 , 32 , 33 , 40 , 49 , 51 ], which we grouped with general-population cohorts, and three cohorts of people with diabetes [ 16 , 21 , 38 ].

all studies that examined loneliness and CVD incidence were conducted in Western countries, limiting the generalizability of their findings [ 21 ].

23.Rationale: While the passage documents high variance ratios for gaseous pollutants (NO2 and O3), it does not interpret higher variance ratios as indicating greater reliability; in fact, high variance ratios reflect larger surrogate variability relative to true personal exposure and are associated with low correlations and large classical error components. The presence of large classical error and low correlations would undermine reliability for long-term epidemiologic analysis rather than support it. The passage does not support the claim that greater surrogate variance makes them more reliable; thus the option's inference is not derivable from the passage.

23.Option: The fact that personal exposure from outdoor sources was estimated using infiltration efficiencies and annual extrapolation suggests that the 'gold-standard' exposure is inherently unreliable, undermining the validity of the entire study's conclusions.
Evidence: Our ‘gold-standard’ exposure to ambient pollution was the personal exposure to pollution from outdoor sources.

To estimate it during the measurement period, we calculated the proportion of ambient levels infiltrating into the home by using the infiltration efficiencies described above when participants were indoors.

The corresponding values for the measurement-period personal exposures were very similar, while the surrogate measures assessing residential outdoor concentrations were higher in magnitude ( Table 1 ).
All measurement campaigns have been through proper quality assurance, quality control (QA/QC) processes and the sensors and methodology used are described elsewhere [ 18–21 ].
23.Rationale: The passage acknowledges that personal measurements are difficult to obtain and describes estimation via infiltration efficiencies and extrapolation. However, it does not claim that this estimated 'gold-standard' is inherently unreliable; on the contrary, it states that measurement-period personal exposures were very similar to the predicted annual personal exposures and documents QA/QC and good sensor agreement. The option's sweeping claim that the study's validity is undermined is not supported by the passage. Therefore this strong negative inference cannot be derived from the provided text.

23.Option: Gaseous pollutants such as NO2 and O3 are more susceptible to classical exposure measurement error, which tends to bias epidemiological associations toward the null, potentially explaining inconsistent or null findings in previous studies.
Evidence: For NO2, the variances of the surrogate estimates were higher compared with the variance of the predicted annual personal exposure from outdoor sources, and the variance ratios ranged from 8.9 for STEAM LHEM-adjusted to 165.0 for STEAM. The Pearson correlation coefficients ranged from 0.08 to 0.25, and the error types were predominantly of classical type (>96% in the mixture).

The errors for O3 were high in magnitude, from 29.7 to 61.2 μg/m3, with a low Pearson correlation between surrogates and personal exposures, high variance ratios (from 35.3 to 52.6), and large classical proportions in the mixture (>94%).

The hypotheses tested in previous theoretical and simulation studies are mainly for classical-type errors for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2).
23.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports that error mixtures for NO2 and O3 are dominated by classical components (>96% for NO2; >94% for O3) and notes that biases from exposure measurement error in simulation studies have generally tended toward the null. Therefore it is epidemiologically reasonable, based on the passage, to infer that gaseous pollutants susceptible to classical error can produce bias toward the null and may help explain inconsistent or null findings in prior studies. This inference follows directly from the documented error types and their known effect on bias described in the passage.

23.Option: Since the LHEM-adjusted surrogates accounted for time–activity and infiltration, they were more accurate and led to higher correlations with personal exposures, suggesting that such adjustments are sufficient to eliminate exposure measurement error in epidemiological studies.
Evidence: The LHEM-adjusted surrogate accounted for the time–activity and indoor concentrations, and thus was more comparable but larger than the predicted annual personal exposures.

The estimated errors for PM2.5 were mixed and the Berkson component was generally larger, from 43% for the nearest-monitor value to 81% for the LHEM-adjusted STEAM estimates, with corresponding variance ratios of 1.3 and 0.2, respectively.
23.Rationale: The passage does state that LHEM-adjusted surrogates (which incorporate time–activity and infiltration) are more comparable to predicted personal exposures and reduce differences. However, it also documents that substantial errors remain (e.g., variance ratios, mixed error types, and substantial Berkson components for some pollutants even after LHEM adjustment). The passage does not claim that LHEM adjustments eliminate exposure measurement error, so concluding that they are sufficient to eliminate ME is not supported. Thus the option's strongest claim (elimination of ME) cannot be derived from the passage.

24.Option: The positive associations between genetically predicted anthropometric traits and CRC-specific mortality were primarily driven by reverse causation and residual confounding, which were effectively mitigated by the Mendelian randomization approach.
Evidence: evidence regarding their association with survival after CRC diagnosis is inconsistent and potentially biased [ 11–16 ].

24.Rationale: The passage states that observational evidence may be biased and that MR is less prone to residual confounding and reverse causation, but it does not assert that the observed positive associations in prior studies were primarily driven by those biases. The MR design reduces these biases, yet the statement that the positive associations 'were primarily driven by reverse causation and residual confounding' is a causal attribution about prior findings that the passage does not provide direct evidence for. Therefore the option overstates what can be derived: the passage supports that MR mitigates such biases, but does not demonstrate that previous associations were primarily due to them.

Evidence: The Genetics and Epidemiology of Colorectal Cancer Consortium (GECCO) and Colon Cancer Family Registry (CCFR) comprise genetic, environmental and survival data from 15 studies of 16 964 individuals of European ancestry (50.3% males, median age at diagnosis; 67 years),

Genetic association estimates for height reaching genome-wide significance (P < 5× 10°−8) were obtained from a meta-analysis of 173 studies of the Genetic Investigation of Anthropometric Traits (GIANT) consortium, including up to 4 080 087 individuals of European ancestry,

In general, positive but imprecisely estimated associations were found for most other anthropometric traits, except for height and birth weight, which yielded null and non-significant inverse results, respectively.
24.Rationale: The passage reports a statistically significant association between genetically predicted higher waist circumference and increased CRC-specific mortality overall. It also reports significant positive associations for hip circumference and BMI in analyses stratified to stage II/III cases. While HC and BMI associations were stage-specific, the passage provides direct evidence that genetically predicted higher WC, HC (stage II/III), and BMI (stage II/III) were associated with higher CRC mortality among CRC cases, supporting the option.

24.Option: The findings suggest that higher body fat percentage and birth weight are protective against CRC-specific mortality, based on the null and inverse associations observed in the study.
Evidence: In general, positive but imprecisely estimated associations were found for most other anthropometric traits, except for height and birth weight, which yielded null and non-significant inverse results, respectively.
24.Rationale: The passage indicates birth weight showed a non-significant inverse result (i.e., point estimate inverse but not statistically significant) and that most other traits (which would include body fat percentage) had positive but imprecise associations. 24.Rationale: After applying bias-correction methods, SIMEX and CWLS produced estimates consistent with the initial IVW result for WC. However, the passage explicitly states that the Slope-hunter method attenuated all association estimates except certain HC and BMI stage II/III results. Because WC is not listed among the exceptions, the Slope-hunter adjustment attenuated the WC association (i.e., rendered it non-robust to that method), supporting the option's claim about lack of robustness to that particular collider-bias adjustment.

25.Option: The observed association between early heavy drinking and increased mortality in men is likely due to reverse causation, as individuals who developed health problems in middle age may have reduced their alcohol intake before study enrolment.
Evidence: these studies classify individuals who have given up drinking due to poor health (‘sick quitters’) within the reference population of non-drinkers [ 10 , 11 ].

The sex-specific results from the analysis excluding the first 2 years of follow-up, without adjusting for BMI or adjusting for Mediterranean diet score were not materially different from the main results ( Supplementary Tables S3–S5 ).

Moreover, the data show that men in the TR5 early-decreasing-heavy group (many of whom quit by age 60) nonetheless had higher mortality (HR 1.18), suggesting the observed association is not merely an artifact of illness-induced reduction in drinking immediately prior to enrolment. Therefore, the claim that the association is likely due to reverse causation is not supported by the passage.

Out of the men with intake data for age 60–69 years, 55% classified as TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ had quit drinking by age 60 years compared with 13% classified as TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’.

For men, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, heavy intake trajectories were associated with higher overall mortality (TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ HR 1.18; 95% CI 1.05–1.32; TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ HR 1.21; 95% CI 1.04–1.40) ( Table 2 ).
25.Rationale: If sustained heavy drinking into later life were the primary driver of increased mortality, one would expect substantially higher risks in the group that continued heavy drinking (TR6) compared with the group that decreased/quit (TR5). However, both TR5 (early decreasing heavy) and TR6 (late decreasing heavy) show similarly elevated overall mortality (HRs 1.18 and 1.21, respectively). TR5 members largely cut down or quit by later ages yet still exhibited increased mortality, indicating that early adulthood heavy drinking carries long-term risk even when not sustained. Therefore, the passage does not support the claim that consequences are primarily driven by sustained heavy drinking into later life.

Evidence: The heavy drinkers among men at age 20–39 years (mean intake ≥60 g/day) tended to either cut down their intake from age 40–49 years and had lower mean intakes compared with TR2 ‘stable light’ drinkers by age 60–69 years (5.4%; TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’)...
Out of the men with intake data for age 60–69 years, 55% classified as TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ had quit drinking by age 60 years compared with 13% classified as TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’.

For men, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, heavy intake trajectories were associated with higher overall mortality (TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ HR 1.18; 95% CI 1.05–1.32; TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ HR 1.21; 95% CI 1.04–1.40) ( Table 2 ).

25.Option: Women who increased their alcohol intake with age had a higher risk of cardiovascular disease-specific mortality, consistent with the protective effect of stable moderate drinking observed in men.
Evidence: For women, 19% higher cancer-specific mortality for TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ (HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.00–1.43)...

Therefore, there is no evidence in the passage that women who increased their intake with age had higher cardiovascular mortality, nor does the passage support the combined claim linking that to a protective effect seen in men. 27.Option: The study's sensitivity analyses suggest that smoking status may have been misclassified, leading to an underestimation of the true association between tuberculosis and COPD.
Evidence: We used smoking status, smoking intensity and cumulative dose to assess the impact of smoking on the association of tuberculosis with risk of COPD.

Therefore the option is not supported by the passage.

When we restricted our analysis to all tuberculosis; only smoking intensity did not modify the association.

27.Rationale: The study adjusted for smoking (status, intensity, cumulative dose) in multivariable models and reports that the association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD persisted after adjustment (Model 3 aHR 1.77). The authors also tested for effect modification and report no evidence that smoking intensity modified the association (P interaction >0.05). Together this supports the inference that the tuberculosis–COPD relationship is not explained away by smoking nor substantially modified by smoking intensity, per the analyses reported in the passage.

27.Option: The high E-values observed in the study suggest that unmeasured confounders, including smoking, could substantially alter the observed association between tuberculosis and COPD.
Evidence: E-values were 2.94 and 1.64 for the associations of pulmonary tuberculosis and all tuberculosis with risk of COPD, respectively.
Model 2 further adjusted for marital status, education level, smoking intensity, alcohol consumption, physical activity and BMI. Model 3 further adjusted for comorbidities and use of medications.
We used smoking status, smoking intensity and cumulative dose to assess the impact of smoking on the association of tuberculosis with risk of COPD.

While E-values quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away an association, the passage does not claim that such confounders exist or that they would substantially change conclusions. Therefore the specific claim in the option is not supported by the passage.

Evidence: The association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD was present in all multivariable models. Hazards ratios, derived from multivariable models measuring the association between pulmonary tuberculosis and COPD, ranged from 2.63 (95% CI, 2.36–2.93) in Model 1 to 1.77 (1.59–1.97) in Model 3 ( Table 2 ).
We used smoking status, smoking intensity and cumulative dose to assess the impact of smoking on the association of tuberculosis with risk of COPD.

We did not find evidence that smoking intensity, sex, alcohol use or physical activity were effect modifiers ( P interaction >0.05) ( Supplementary Tables S7 and S8 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online).

When using differing classifications of smoking ( Supplementary Table S5 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online) in model adjustments or a three-category variable for tuberculosis ( Supplementary Table S6 , available as Supplementary data at IJE online), results were similar.
27.Rationale: If smoking were the primary driver of the observed tuberculosis–COPD association, adjustment for smoking would be expected to eliminate or greatly attenuate the association. However, the adjusted association remained statistically significant in fully adjusted models (Model 3 aHR 1.77). The authors also report that smoking intensity did not modify the association and that differing smoking classifications yielded similar results. Thus the passage does not support the claim that smoking is the primary driver or that the observed association is largely attributable to smoking.

28.Option: In settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 cases per 100,000 person-years, the actual proportion of TB cases in household contacts attributable to household transmission likely exceeds the estimated 61%.
Evidence: However, this assumption may be challenged, as some HHCs likely acquire TB infections from community sources, introducing the non-differential misclassification of TB outcomes [ 1–5 ].
In principle, such non-differential misclassification biases study results toward the null, underestimating the true magnitude of the associations.

28.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that some household contacts acquire infection from community sources, producing non-differential misclassification that biases results toward the null and thus underestimates true associations. The spline model yields an estimated matching proportion of ≥61% in settings with incidence ≤250/100,000, but given the stated tendency for misclassification to underestimate household transmission and the documented methodological gaps (including delayed ascertainment and incomplete follow-up), it is epidemiologically reasonable to infer that the true proportion attributable to within-household transmission likely exceeds the observed/estimated 61%.

28.Option: The 61% genetic linkage estimate in low-to-moderate TB incidence settings may be inflated due to the inclusion of co-prevalent cases, which are more likely to represent community transmission than household transmission.
Evidence: Twenty-six of 51 (51%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 55 of 94 (59%) index–secondary pairs were genetically linked.

Transmission was observed in 34 of 66 (52%, 95% CI: 39%–64%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 74 of 109 (68%, 95% CI: 58%–77%) index–secondary pairs, with most secondary pairs (72/74) differing by up to five SNPs.
In principle, such non-differential misclassification biases study results toward the null, underestimating the true magnitude of the associations.
28.Rationale: The option claims the 61% estimate may be inflated by inclusion of co-prevalent cases that are more likely community-acquired. The passage data show that co-prevalent pairs had lower proportions of genetic linkage (about 51%–52%) than secondary pairs (about 59%–68%), consistent with co-prevalent cases being less often genetically linked to the index (i.e., more likely community-acquired). Moreover, the authors state that non-differential misclassification from community-acquired infections biases estimates toward the null (underestimation), not inflation. Therefore, inclusion of co-prevalent cases would be expected to lower, not inflate, the overall matching proportion; the contention that the 61% estimate is inflated by inclusion of co-prevalent cases is not supported by the passage.

29.Option: The finding of a recent increase in CHD and stroke mortality in Australian and New Zealand GBD estimates is chiefly attributable to the use of projected mortality data from 2016.
Evidence: GBD 2019 estimates showed decreases in age-standardized CVD mortality rates from 1990 to 2013 for Australia and New Zealand and slight increases from 2013 to 2019 [ 8 ]. However, since official cause-specific mortality data were only available up to 2015 (New Zealand)/2016 (Australia) at the time of publishing, GBD estimates for 2016/17–2019 were projections rather than observed data.

GBD estimates showed average annual decreases in CVD mortality of 5.9% (5.2%–6.5%) during 2008–12, and 2.8% (1.8%–3.8%) during 2012–16, with annual increases of 1.2% (0.2%–2.2%) during 2016–19 ( Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table S2 ).

In 2016 (the last year with observed data in GBD), GBD estimates were 3.2% higher than official national data (136.5 versus 132.3 per 100 000), widening to 17.6% higher (140.8 versus 119.7 per 100 000 people) in 2019 ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), suggesting out-of-sample predictions largely contributed to the observed differences.
29.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that GBD had no observed input data beyond 2016/2015 for Australia/New Zealand and therefore produced out-of-sample projections for 2016/17–2019. The GBD estimates show increases during 2016–19 and the authors state that out-of-sample predictions largely contributed to the divergence between GBD and official data. Therefore the explanation that the recent increase in GBD estimates is chiefly attributable to use of projected (out-of-sample) data is directly supported by the Passage Body.

29.Option: The slowing in CVD mortality decline observed in official national data may be due to increasing prevalence of risk factors such as diabetes and obesity, which have lagged effects on cardiovascular outcomes.
Evidence: The suggestion of stagnating or increasing CVD mortality raises serious concerns, particularly for chronic disease policy and practice, and achievement of non-communicable disease goals [ 10 ].

In Australia and New Zealand, although multiple causes of death are listed on death certificates, official mortality data focus on the underlying cause of death, referring to the primary condition initiating events leading to death [ 6 , 7 ]. This approach supports consistent monitoring of conditions like CVD over time.
29.Rationale: The passage notes concern about stagnating or increasing CVD mortality and describes data sources and methods, but it does not present evidence linking the observed slowing to specific risk-factor trends (e.g. diabetes or obesity) or provide data on those prevalence trends. The statement attributes causation to increasing prevalence of particular risk factors, which is not supported by any quotation or analysis in the Passage Body. Therefore this inference cannot be derived from the provided text.

29.Option: The differences in CVD mortality estimates between official national data and GBD are primarily due to variations in data collection methods and definitions of underlying cause of death.
Evidence: In Australia and New Zealand, although multiple causes of death are listed on death certificates, official mortality data focus on the underlying cause of death, referring to the primary condition initiating events leading to death [ 6 , 7 ]. This approach supports consistent monitoring of conditions like CVD over time.

The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Collaboration, which also uses the underlying cause of death to classify mortality [ 8 ], is a highly regarded initiative that synthesizes a large number of data sources to estimate mortality, causes of death and illness, and risk factors and provides comprehensive assessments of trends over time and by country.

Data are processed—including for cause of death redistribution and correction for non-reference case definitions or measurement methods—and modelled using standardized tools including Cause of Death Ensemble model (CODEm), spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression, and DisMod-MR to generate estimates of each measure of interest by age, sex, location, and year [ 8 ].
GBD data processing redistributes 'ill-defined' causes of death (e.g. heart failure [ICD-10 code I50]) to causes with greater policy utility [ 8 , 18 ].
29.Rationale: The passage indicates that both official national data and GBD use the underlying cause of death approach, so differences are not primarily due to differing definitions of underlying cause. Instead, the passage attributes divergence to GBD-specific data processing (redistribution of ill-defined causes), corrections, and modelling (including out-of-sample projections). While variations in data collection could play a role, the Passage Body emphasizes processing/modeling and projection differences rather than fundamental differences in the definition of underlying cause, so the option as stated is not supported as the primary explanation.

29.Option: The redistribution of ill-defined causes of death used by the GBD may have contributed to higher absolute CHD mortality rates in GBD estimates compared to official national data.
Evidence: Data are processed—including for cause of death redistribution and correction for non-reference case definitions or measurement methods—and modelled using standardized tools including Cause of Death Ensemble model (CODEm), spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression, and DisMod-MR to generate estimates of each measure of interest by age, sex, location, and year [ 8 ].
GBD data processing redistributes 'ill-defined' causes of death (e.g. heart failure [ICD-10 code I50]) to causes with greater policy utility [ 8 , 18 ].

GBD estimates also showed an overall decrease in age-standardized CHD mortality rates from 2008 (104.7 per 100 000 people) to 2019 (75.8 per 100 000), with absolute rates considerably higher than those from national mortality data ( Fig. 1 ).
29.Rationale: The passage documents that GBD explicitly redistributes ill-defined causes of death to more specific causes and that GBD's absolute CHD mortality rates are considerably higher than official national rates. The cautious phrasing 'may have contributed' is warranted: redistribution of ill-defined causes is a described GBD processing step that plausibly increases assigned deaths to specific causes like CHD, so it is a supported explanation for higher absolute GBD CHD rates in the Passage Body.

29.Option: The apparent stabilization of stroke mortality in GBD estimates for Australia and New Zealand is due to the GBD's use of spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression, which smooths out short-term fluctuations in mortality data.
Evidence: Data are processed—including for cause of death redistribution and correction for non-reference case definitions or measurement methods—and modelled using standardized tools including Cause of Death Ensemble model (CODEm), spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression, and DisMod-MR to generate estimates of each measure of interest by age, sex, location, and year [ 8 ].

For GBD estimates, Joinpoint analysis results showed a 4.5% (95% CI: 4.0%–5.0%) average annual decline in stroke mortality during 2008–13, with no statistically significant changes between 2013–16 and 2016–19 ( Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table S3 ).

59.Option: Neighbourhood walkability, as measured by intersection density, is a strong predictor of lower BMI in Latin American cities, similar to findings in high-income countries.
Evidence: many studies that evaluated indicators of street connectivity or walkability such as intersection density at the neighbourhood level demonstrate an association with a higher likelihood of walking and physical activity [ 7 ] and also an inverse association with BMI or obesity [ 8 ].
For intersection density (Models 2b and 3), associations with BMI were null among men and women in all countries.
59.Rationale: The passage contrasts prior findings from high-income settings (where intersection density is inversely associated with BMI) with the study's results showing no association between intersection density and BMI in any country or gender in this Latin American sample. Thus the claim that intersection density is a strong predictor of lower BMI in these cities is not supported by the study's findings.

59.Option: In Latin American cities, higher neighbourhood education is consistently associated with lower BMI across all countries and genders, mirroring patterns observed in high-income countries.
Evidence: Most of these studies have shown that individual and neighbourhood SEPs are independently and inversely associated with BMI.

There are inverse associations between neighbourhood education and BMI in Argentina and Chile for both men and women, even after adjusting for individual and city characteristics (Models 1 and 2a, Figures 1 and 2 ).
In Colombia and Mexico, we also observe inverse associations between neighbourhood education and BMI among women but the associations are weaker.

In contrast, among men living in Colombia and Mexico, we observe a pattern in the opposite direction, with a 1-SD higher unit in neighbourhood education being associated with 0.456 (CI 0.224, 0.689) and 0.177 (CI 0.058, 0.295) kg/m 2 higher BMI in men from Colombia and Mexico, respectively (Model 2a; individual education model).
59.Rationale: While high-income country studies and some countries in this analysis (Argentina, Chile) show inverse associations, the study documents heterogeneity: associations are weaker among women in Colombia and Mexico and are actually positive among men in Colombia and Mexico. Therefore, a statement of consistent inverse associations across all countries and genders is not supported by the presented results.

59.Option: The association between neighbourhood green space and BMI is universally inverse across Latin American cities, consistent with patterns observed in high-income countries.
Evidence: Neighbourhood greenness has also been found to be inversely associated with overweight indicators [ 9 ].

For neighbourhood greenness, after adjusting for individual education (Model 2c), associations with BMI among men and women were null in Chile, slightly positive in Argentina (women β 0.132; CI 0.009, 0.255), and negative in Mexico [1-SD higher unit in neighbourhood greenness associated with 0.187 (CI –0.304, –0.070) and 0.185 (CI –0.306, –0.064) lower BMI in men and women, respectively] and Colombia (although weaker).
When adjusting for multiple exposures (Models 3), associations were attenuated to the null in Argentina and to a lesser extent in Mexico ( Figures 1 and 2 , and Supplementary Tables S5 and S6 ).
59.Rationale: Although prior literature often shows inverse associations between greenness and overweight, the study's findings in Latin American cities are mixed: null in Chile, slightly positive in Argentina (for women), and negative in Mexico and Colombia (with varying strength), and some associations attenuate with adjustment. Thus a universal inverse relationship across the region is not supported by the data.

59.Option: Neighbourhood characteristics in Latin America appear to influence BMI differently from those in the Global North, reinforcing the need for the generation of further evidence on residential associations in these settings.
Evidence: Most studies on neighbourhood features and BMI have been conducted in high-income countries in the Global North and it is unclear whether these patterns of associations are also observed in other regions of the world.

We expect to find different associations in Latin American cities compared with those of the Global North given the faster pace of urbanization and that neighbourhood environments are more heterogeneous.

There are inverse associations between neighbourhood education and BMI in Argentina and Chile for both men and women, even after adjusting for individual and city characteristics (Models 1 and 2a, Figures 1 and 2 ).

In Colombia and Mexico, we also observe inverse associations between neighbourhood education and BMI among women but the associations are weaker. In contrast, among men living in Colombia and Mexico, we observe a pattern in the opposite direction...
For intersection density (Models 2b and 3), associations with BMI were null among men and women in all countries.
59.Rationale: The passage explicitly notes uncertainty about whether Global North patterns apply elsewhere and hypothesizes different associations in Latin America. The study's results demonstrate heterogeneity and some patterns that diverge from established findings (e.g., null intersection density associations; country- and gender-specific differences in neighbourhood education effects), supporting the inference that neighbourhood influences differ in Latin America and that more context-specific evidence is needed.

61.Option: The method reduces bias from horizontal pleiotropy by using genetic instruments that are unlikely to exhibit indirect genetic effects, thereby improving the validity of causal estimates.
Evidence: This can be mitigated by selecting genetic instruments that are unlikely to exhibit indirect genetic effects.

Application of the MR gene-by-environment (GxE) by stratifying on spousal parity (i.e. inclusion and comparison to spousal pairs who do not have children) can provide evidence for violation of the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions and enable estimation of the causal effect of the exposure on the outcome, correcting for such violations [ 23–25 ].

The presence of a (spurious) “causal” association between the genetic instrument and the outcome in nulliparous spousal pairs can be used to quantify the degree of horizontal pleiotropy and confounding present in the analysis, and to subsequently correct any causal estimates for pleiotropy in parous spousal pairs.
61.Rationale: While the passage explicitly states that selecting genetic instruments unlikely to exhibit indirect genetic effects can mitigate bias (quote 1), this is described as a mitigation strategy rather than the unique methodological feature of the proposed framework. The passage identifies the novel, unique feature as the GxE stratification on spousal parity (inclusion and comparison of nulliparous spousal pairs) that provides direct evidence for violations (quotes 2–3). Therefore, Option 0 describes a general instrument-selection tactic present in many MR studies, not the unique framework element that addresses the specific systematic error described in the question.

61.Option: The inclusion of nulliparous spousal pairs allows for the detection of horizontal pleiotropy through the offspring genome, enabling correction of causal estimates in parous pairs.
Evidence: Application of the MR gene-by-environment (GxE) by stratifying on spousal parity (i.e. inclusion and comparison to spousal pairs who do not have children) can provide evidence for violation of the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions and enable estimation of the causal effect of the exposure on the outcome, correcting for such violations [ 23–25 ].
Here, nulliparous spousal pairs effectively act as negative controls, allowing for the identification of heterogeneity in effect estimates owing to non-causal influences.

The presence of a (spurious) “causal” association between the genetic instrument and the outcome in nulliparous spousal pairs can be used to quantify the degree of horizontal pleiotropy and confounding present in the analysis, and to subsequently correct any causal estimates for pleiotropy in parous spousal pairs.
61.Rationale: The passage explicitly describes using nulliparous spousal pairs as negative controls within a GxE framework to detect non-causal associations (including horizontal pleiotropy) and to quantify and correct for pleiotropy when estimating causal effects in parous pairs. These sentences directly support the inference in Option 1.

61.Option: Unlike most traditional MR studies, our framework includes an inbuilt control for violation of core assumptions through the inclusion and comparison of causal effect estimates derived from spousal pairs who do not have children.
Evidence: Application of the MR gene-by-environment (GxE) by stratifying on spousal parity (i.e. inclusion and comparison to spousal pairs who do not have children) can provide evidence for violation of the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions and enable estimation of the causal effect of the exposure on the outcome, correcting for such violations [ 23–25 ].
Here, nulliparous spousal pairs effectively act as negative controls, allowing for the identification of heterogeneity in effect estimates owing to non-causal influences.

For example, if the offspring exposure is causal for the maternal health outcome, then genetic instruments for the exposure in the father should only be associated with maternal outcomes in spousal pairs who have shared an offspring. Conversely, the “offspring” exposure could not plausibly influence the outcome in nulliparous pairs.
61.Rationale: The passage states that stratifying on spousal parity (including and comparing nulliparous spousal pairs) provides evidence for violations of MR core assumptions (independence and exclusion restriction) and enables correction of causal estimates. This constitutes an inbuilt control for assumption violations that distinguishes the proposed framework from many traditional MR designs and directly matches the statement in Option 2.

62.Option: In settings with typical malaria endemicity, the positive predictive value of the WHO clinical pneumonia definition is approximately 70%, primarily due to a high proportion of misclassified cases.
Evidence: Based on our model, we estimate that, in a region with a typical malaria parasitaemia prevalence of 24% [ 17 ], 47.8% of WHO pneumonia cases are malaria-slide-negative, 24.6% are coinfected, and 27.6% are misclassified ( Figure 3 ). This corresponds to a PPV of 72.4%.
62.Rationale: The passage explicitly provides modelled estimates for a typical malaria parasitaemia prevalence (24%) showing a PPV of 72.4%, which is approximately 70%. The same sentence shows that a large fraction of WHO-defined cases are misclassified (27.6%), which substantially lowers PPV in these settings. Therefore the statement is directly supported by the Passage Body.

62.Option: The presence of crackles on chest auscultation and lower chest wall indrawing in malaria-positive children with pneumonia symptoms is sufficient to confirm radiological pneumonia and rule out misclassification.
Evidence: The most important associations with CXR-positivity were, in rank order: lower chest wall indrawing [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) =18.1, 95% confidence interval (95% CI): 1.9, 175.8, P = 0.012], crackles on chest auscultation (aOR =13.1, 95% CI: 1.4, 127.4, P = 0.027), and nasal flaring (aOR =5.9, 95% CI: 1.1, 32.8, P = 0.041). CXR-positivity was negatively associated with multiple or prolonged convulsions (aOR = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.02, 0.95, P = 0.044).
62.Rationale: The passage reports strong associations (adjusted odds ratios) between certain clinical signs and CXR-positivity, but association does not equate to sufficiency or perfect diagnostic confirmation. The authors do not claim that these signs are sufficient to 'confirm' radiological pneumonia or to 'rule out' misclassification; they report probabilistic associations only. Thus the definitive claim of sufficiency is not supported by the Passage Body.

62.Option: The WHO clinical pneumonia definition has high specificity in all settings, as confirmed by the 97.5% positive predictive value observed in the PERCH study.
Evidence: In developing the original pneumonia case definitions, the WHO prioritized sensitivity to ensure that no child who might benefit from antibiotics is denied treatment [ 15 ]. However, the trade-off for high sensitivity was poor specificity: many children who do not have pneumonia are also captured by the case definition.

By applying the three assumptions outlined in the Methods and Figure 1 , we estimated that, among PERCH cases that met the WHO pneumonia criteria, 95.3% were malaria-slide-negative (and true pneumonia cases), 2.2% were coinfected (malaria-slide-positive with pneumonia), and 2.5% were misclassified (malaria-slide-positive without pneumonia). Therefore, the PPV was calculated as 97.5% (95.3% + 2.2%).
62.Rationale: The passage states that WHO case definitions were designed to prioritize sensitivity and that this comes at the cost of poor specificity, directly contradicting the blanket claim of high specificity in all settings. Moreover, the 97.5% PPV reported applies to the specific PERCH cases under the study assumptions and is not a direct measure of specificity nor generalizable to all settings (PPV depends on prevalence). Therefore the option overstates what can be inferred from the Passage Body.

62.Option: The decline in clinical pneumonia cases in Kilifi, Kenya, between 2002 and 2011 was primarily due to improved access to antibiotics and better healthcare infrastructure.
Evidence: PERCH was a case–control study that was conducted between August 2011 and January 2014 in seven low- and middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. This analysis is restricted to three sites that were malaria-endemic, i.e. Kilifi, Kenya; Basse, The Gambia; and Bamako, Mali.
62.Rationale: The Passage Body describes the PERCH study sites (including Kilifi) and study methods but contains no data or statements about a decline in clinical pneumonia cases in Kilifi from 2002–2011, nor any attribution of trends to improved antibiotics access or infrastructure. Because the passage provides no evidence about such a decline or its causes, this causal assertion cannot be derived from the Passage Body.

62.Option: The model used in the study assumes that malaria parasitaemia prevalence and clinical pneumonia incidence are inversely related, which explains the observed decline in pneumonia cases in Kilifi.
Evidence: Let λ denote the average rate of WHO pneumonia across the PERCH sites and u denote the prevalence of malaria parasitaemia in the PERCH controls. Among members of the PERCH communities that were negative for malaria parasitaemia, the expected rate of malaria-slide-negative WHO pneumonia cases (Group 1) is λ p1 / ( 1 - u ). Similarly, among community members that were positive for malaria parasitaemia, the expected rates of coinfected (Group 2) and misclassified (Group 3) WHO pneumonia cases are λ p2 / u and λ p3 / u , respectively.

Based on our model, we estimate that, in a region with a typical malaria parasitaemia prevalence of 24% [ 17 ], 47.8% of WHO pneumonia cases are malaria-slide-negative, 24.6% are coinfected, and 27.6% are misclassified ( Figure 3 ). This corresponds to a PPV of 72.4%.
62.Rationale: The model describes how expected rates depend on λ (pneumonia rate) and u (malaria parasitaemia prevalence) and uses these to compute PPV; it does not assume an inverse relationship between u and λ. The passage also does not report an 'observed decline' in pneumonia cases in Kilifi nor attribute any decline to this modeled relationship. Therefore the option's claim about model assumptions and explanation for a decline is not supported by the Passage Body.

63.Option: For some groups, life expectancy losses in 2020 were driven primarily by increases in mortality from 'other' causes, reflecting the syndemic interplay of COVID-19, endemic diseases, and social determinants of health.
Evidence: COVID-19 has been conceptualized as a syndemic [ 12–16 ], characterized by: (1) clustering of multiple diseases or health conditions within a population or context, (2) adverse interactions between these conditions resulting in worse health, ‘and’ (3) social, political, or environmental factors that further exacerbate the disease/disease interactions [ 12 , 17 ].

Importantly, education played a key role in non-COVID-19 mortality. Nearly all LE losses among high-education Hispanic and White individuals were due to COVID-19, whereas for low-education White and Black individuals, COVID-19 only accounted for 40%–47% of losses.
In each subgroup of race/ethnicity and sex, individuals with low education lost −1.3 to −2.5 years (22%–60%) from combined non-COVID-19 causes.
Black men with low and medium education and Black women with low education lost the most LE from non-COVID-19 causes (−2.5 to −2.6 years, 53%–56%).
63.Rationale: The passage explicitly frames COVID-19 as a syndemic (quote 1) and provides data showing that for some subgroups—particularly low-education Black and White individuals—a substantial or majority portion of 2020 life expectancy (LE) losses came from non-COVID causes (quotes 2–4). This supports the inference that, for those groups, LE declines were driven primarily by increases in other causes of death and that these patterns reflect interactions among COVID-19, preexisting endemic diseases, and social determinants of health.

63.Option: The socioeconomic gradient in life expectancy losses was primarily driven by disparities in access to healthcare, particularly for individuals with low education and racial and ethnic minority backgrounds.
Evidence: unequal health insurance coverage left 28 million US citizens uninsured or underinsured in 2020 [ 24 ], disproportionately affecting socioeconomically deprived populations and racial and ethnic minorities [ 25 ].

COVID-19 has been conceptualized as a syndemic [ 12–16 ], characterized by: (1) clustering of multiple diseases or health conditions within a population or context, (2) adverse interactions between these conditions resulting in worse health, ‘and’ (3) social, political, or environmental factors that further exacerbate the disease/disease interactions [ 12 , 17 ].
In each subgroup of race/ethnicity and sex, individuals with low education lost −1.3 to −2.5 years (22%–60%) from combined non-COVID-19 causes.
63.Rationale: While the passage documents a socioeconomic gradient in LE losses and mentions unequal health insurance coverage affecting deprived and minority populations (quote 1) as one social determinant, it does not provide evidence that disparities in access to healthcare were the primary driver of the gradient. The authors describe multiple interacting mechanisms (syndemic factors including comorbidities, behavioral risks, exposure risks, and broader social determinants—quote 2) and present cause-specific mortality patterns (quote 3). The passage therefore does not support the stronger claim that healthcare access disparities were the primary (i.e., single main) driver of the socioeconomic gradient in LE losses.

63.Option: The rise in life expectancy losses from deaths of despair in 2020 and 2021 was primarily due to increased access to mental health services among low-SES individuals during the pandemic.
Evidence: Deaths of despair heavily impacted White and Black men with low education and Black men with middle education, with LE losses of −0.4 to −0.6 years (9%–23%). Low-education White women lost −0.4 years (15%) due to deaths of despair.
From 2020 to 2021, ... For non-COVID-19 causes, deaths of despair were the leading contributors to LE losses across population subgroups, followed by unintentional injuries.
63.Rationale: The passage documents increased LE losses due to deaths of despair in 2020 and 2021 across several low-education subgroups (quotes). However, it contains no evidence that these increases were caused by increased access to mental health services; in fact, increased access to services would be an implausible causal explanation for rising deaths of despair. Because the passage does not provide support for the asserted causal mechanism (increased access to mental health services), the statement cannot be derived from the presented evidence.

63.Option: LE gains observed among Hispanic individuals with high and middle education in 2020 were primarily due to protective factors that mitigated the negative impacts of the syndemic on non-communicable diseases.
Evidence: By contrast, Hispanic men and women with high and middle education experienced some LE ‘gains’ in 2020, mainly from NCDs. For example, Hispanic men with high education experienced LE gains of about two years from NCDs.

COVID-19 has been conceptualized as a syndemic [ 12–16 ], characterized by: (1) clustering of multiple diseases or health conditions within a population or context, (2) adverse interactions between these conditions resulting in worse health, ‘and’ (3) social, political, or environmental factors that further exacerbate the disease/disease interactions [ 12 , 17 ].
63.Rationale: The passage reports that high- and middle-education Hispanic individuals experienced LE gains in 2020 mainly attributable to non-communicable diseases (NCDs) (quote 1). However, it does not identify or provide evidence that these gains were 'primarily due to protective factors' that mitigated syndemic impacts; no specific protective mechanisms are described. Thus the specific causal interpretation (primary role of protective factors mitigating syndemic effects) is not supported by the passage and cannot be reliably inferred.

64.Option: Women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage were at an increased risk of multiple myeloma, regardless of educational attainment, even after adjusting for individual-level socioeconomic factors and body mass index.
Evidence: Women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage had a 51% increase in the incidence of MM (Quartile 4 vs Quartile 1, HR: 1.51, 95% CI: 1.06, 2.15, P trend: .002 and HR: 1.48, 95% CI: 1.02, 2.13, P trend: .003) in age-adjusted and MV-adjusted analyses, respectively (the change in estimates was primarily affected by the inclusion of BMI in the MV models).
We fit Cox proportional hazards regression models, stratified by age and follow-up period and adjusted for covariates, to evaluate whether nDIS or nSES was associated with MM incidence.
The results stratified by educational attainment are presented in Table 3.

Positive associations of neighborhood disadvantage and MM risk were apparent among women with ≤12 years of formal education and those with at least some college: age-adjusted HR was 1.87 (95% CI: 1.00, 3.48) and slightly attenuated in MV-adjusted models (HR: 1.79, 95% CI: 0.95, 3.37) for high vs low nDIS, respectively.
No association was observed among women with ≤12 years of formal education (Table 3).
64.Rationale: The passage does support an overall increased MM incidence for women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage after multivariable adjustment (HR ~1.48, 95% CI excludes 1). However, the claim that this increase applies "regardless of educational attainment" is not supported by the stratified results. The study presents stratified analyses by education that show differing estimates (and even an explicit statement of no association in one educational stratum), so one cannot infer that the increased risk is uniform across educational groups. Therefore the part of the option claiming "regardless of educational attainment" is not derivable from the passage.

64.Option: The lack of statistical significance in the nSES association (HR: 1.35, 95% CI: 0.93, 1.96, P trend: .14) suggests that neighborhood socioeconomic status has no meaningful association with multiple myeloma incidence among Black women.
Evidence: We also observed a 35% higher incidence of MM among women living in areas of low nSES compared with those in areas of high nSES (HR: 1.35, 95% CI: 0.93, 1.96, P trend: .14).
Again, the results were similar in fully adjusted models (HR: 1.28, 95% CI: 0.87, 1.90, P trend: .31).
64.Rationale: The passage reports a positive point estimate for low nSES (HR > 1) but with 95% CIs that include 1 and P-values > 0.05. A non-statistically significant result does not permit the strong conclusion that there is "no meaningful association." The data are compatible with a modest positive association (point estimates >1) but the study lacked sufficient precision to rule out no effect. The passage itself reports the elevated HRs and notes they are not statistically significant; it does not conclude there is no meaningful association, so the option overstates what can be inferred.

64.Option: The increased risk of multiple myeloma among Black women living in disadvantaged neighborhoods is likely due to unmeasured genetic factors related to racial ancestry, as disparities in MM incidence are not explained by genetic ancestry.
Evidence: Although factors underlying the differences in MM incidence by race are not fully understood, disparities do not appear to be explained by genetic ancestry [ 6 ].
Instead, differences by race may be influenced by a combination of social and neighborhood-level factors, including environmental exposures and socioeconomic conditions.

Women living in areas of concentrated disadvantage had a 51% increase in the incidence of MM ... in age-adjusted and MV-adjusted analyses, respectively (the change in estimates was primarily affected by the inclusion of BMI in the MV models).
64.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that disparities do not appear to be explained by genetic ancestry and instead highlights social and neighborhood-level factors as plausible explanations. Therefore, attributing the increased risk primarily to unmeasured genetic factors contradicts the text. The evidence supports sociostructural and environmental explanations rather than implicating genetic ancestry as the likely cause.

64.Option: The association between neighborhood socioeconomic context and multiple myeloma incidence is primarily driven by differences in individual-level educational attainment, as the observed risk was only significant among women with less than a high school education.
Evidence: We fit Cox proportional hazards regression models, stratified by age and follow-up period and adjusted for covariates, to evaluate whether nDIS or nSES was associated with MM incidence.

Multivariable (MV) models were additionally adjusted for cumulative average BMI (<25, 25–29, 30–34, ≥35 kg/m2), educational attainment (<=12, 13–15, >=16 years), alcohol consumption (<1, 1–6, >=7 drinks/week), cigarette smoking (current, past, never), physical activity (none, <5, >=5 hours/week), and region of residence (Northeast, South, Midwest, West).
The results stratified by educational attainment are presented in Table 3.

Positive associations of neighborhood disadvantage and MM risk were apparent among women with ≤12 years of formal education and those with at least some college: age-adjusted HR was 1.87 (95% CI: 1.00, 3.48) and slightly attenuated in MV-adjusted models (HR: 1.79, 95% CI: 0.95, 3.37) for high vs low nDIS, respectively.
HRs in the strata of completing some college were 1.20 in both the age-adjusted and MV-adjusted models.
No association was observed among women with ≤12 years of formal education (Table 3).
64.Rationale: The MV models adjusted for educational attainment and still showed an overall association between neighborhood disadvantage and MM, so the association is not explained solely by individual-level education. The stratified findings do not consistently show that the effect is "only significant" among women with less than a high school education; the stratified estimates vary and the passage includes inconsistent statements about which strata show associations. Thus, the claim that the association is primarily driven by individual educational attainment and is only significant among the lowest education group is not supported by the presented results.

64.Option: Residence in disadvantaged neighborhoods has been linked to lower walkability scores and reduced physical activity, which may contribute to higher rates of obesity and, in turn, increase the risk of multiple myeloma incidence among Black women.
Evidence: Obesity [ 7 ] and pesticides (usually via occupational exposure) [ 8–11 ] are the most consistent established modifiable risk factors for MM.
Living in areas of disadvantage puts people at a higher risk of being exposed to obesogenic environments.

Two studies based in New York City reported inverse associations between neighborhood walkability—which is associated with increased levels of physical activity and lower rates of obesity [ 23 , 24 ]—and MM incidence;

Participants who lived in areas with the highest concentrated disadvantage were more likely to be obese (36% vs 22%) ... and less likely to ... engage in physical activity (55% vs 65%) compared with those in areas of lowest disadvantage.
64.Rationale: The passage establishes obesity as a recognized modifiable risk factor for MM and states that disadvantaged neighborhoods are obesogenic and have lower physical activity levels; it also cites prior studies linking lower walkability to higher MM incidence. The cohort data show higher obesity prevalence and lower physical activity among residents of high-disadvantage neighborhoods, and the authors note that inclusion of BMI affected estimates. Together, these pieces of evidence support the plausible inference (stated cautiously as "may contribute") that lower walkability and reduced activity in disadvantaged neighborhoods could contribute to obesity and thereby to increased MM risk among Black women.

65.Option: The improvement in timely administration of birth dose vaccines during the intervention period was primarily due to the John-Henry effect, where participants in the control period worked harder to compensate for not receiving the intervention, thereby influencing the outcome.
Evidence: By default, it was difficult to blind the study participants, investigators, and data collectors to the intervention so the trial was open-label.
During the control period, participants received the standard maternal, newborn, and child health care package provided by health workers.

During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG administration were 93%, 92.7%, and 92.1% compared to 80.9%, 81.6%, and 77.9% during the control period, respectively ( P < .001).
65.Rationale: The passage describes an open-label trial and defines the control condition as receiving standard care, and it reports improved timeliness during the intervention period. However, there is no information or evidence in the passage that participants in the control period 'worked harder' or engaged in compensatory behaviors (John‑Henry effect). The open-label design alone does not provide proof of such compensatory behavior. Because the passage contains no statements or data indicating a John‑Henry effect, the causal claim that the improvement was 'primarily due' to that effect cannot be derived from the passage.

65.Option: The trend toward better timeliness in birth dose vaccines during the intervention period might be explained by the low intervention intensity as only three standardized text message reminders were sent to the participants and the shorter transition time between the intervention and control periods.
Evidence: The participants received three standardized text message reminders notifying them to consider taking their babies for timely vaccination during the intervention period. The first text message reminder was sent upon registration, the second was sent two weeks before the expected delivery date, and the last was sent on the expected date of delivery.
The intervention was text message reminders provided to all participants in a phased manner, with the transition from the control period to the intervention period being every two months.

During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG administration were 93%, 92.7%, and 92.1% compared to 80.9%, 81.6%, and 77.9% during the control period, respectively ( P < .001).
65.Rationale: The passage does state that the intervention consisted of three standardized text reminders and that transitions occurred every two months. However, the claim that the observed 'trend' toward better timeliness 'might be explained' by 'low intervention intensity' and 'shorter transition time' is speculative and not supported by data or analysis in the passage. The passage does not present any comparison of different intervention intensities, nor does it analyze the effect of transition timing on outcomes. Therefore, while the factual elements cited are present, the causal explanation proposed is not derivable from the supplied evidence.

65.Option: The findings are limited to a shorter intervention period, so the long-term intervention effects remain unknown, which undermines the validity of the trial's conclusions about the effectiveness of text message reminders.
Evidence: We conducted an open-label, stepped-wedge cluster-randomized pilot trial between December 2019 and April 2020 in the Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County in Kenya [ 8 ].
This trial was not registered as it was a pilot.
The data were collected through cross-sectional surveys from a random sample of participants who received the text message intervention.

During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0 administration (adjusted RR [aRR] 1.16, 95% CI: 1.00–1.35), BCG (aRR 1.14, 95% CI: 0.98–1.33), and OPV or BCG (aRR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.00–1.43) tended to improve compared to the control period, adjusting for other factors.
65.Rationale: It is supported by the passage that this was a pilot trial with a defined, relatively short date range (Dec 2019–Apr 2020) and that data were collected cross‑sectionally, so the long‑term durability of effects beyond the study period is not reported and therefore remains unknown. However, the statement that this uncertainty 'undermines the validity of the trial's conclusions about the effectiveness' overstates what can be derived: the trial provides internally valid evidence of short‑term effects during the study period (with reported aRRs and P‑values). The passage does not present evidence showing that short duration invalidates the observed short‑term effect estimates. Therefore, while the lack of long‑term follow‑up is a limitation that leaves long‑term effects unspecified, claiming it undermines the trial's validity is not supported by the passage.

65.Option: Text message reminders improved the timely administration of birth dose vaccines among newborns in an informal urban settlement, suggesting they could serve as an additional tool for improving vaccination program performance in similar settings.
Evidence: We conducted an open-label, stepped-wedge cluster-randomized pilot trial between December 2019 and April 2020 in the Viwandani urban informal settlement in Nairobi County in Kenya [ 8 ].
Viwandani is composed of a mobile population..., characterized by poor uptake of and access to health services, especially vaccination [ 11 , 12 ].

Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home. We leveraged the widespread use of mobile phones and text reminders as a low-cost intervention to nudge parents toward timely vaccinations, ultimately increasing immunization rates.

During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0, BCG, and OPV 0 and BCG administration were 93%, 92.7%, and 92.1% compared to 80.9%, 81.6%, and 77.9% during the control period, respectively ( P < .001).

During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0 administration (adjusted RR [aRR] 1.16, 95% CI: 1.00–1.35), BCG (aRR 1.14, 95% CI: 0.98–1.33), and OPV or BCG (aRR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.00–1.43) tended to improve compared to the control period, adjusting for other factors.
65.Rationale: The passage reports a stepped‑wedge pilot trial conducted in a high‑mobility urban informal settlement (Viwandani) and documents higher timely administration percentages and adjusted risk ratios during the intervention period. The authors also describe the plausible mechanism (text reminders addressing forgetfulness and reaching mobile caregivers) and frame the intervention as a low‑cost nudge to increase immunization rates. From these data and context, it is reasonable to infer that text message reminders improved timeliness in this setting and therefore could serve as an additional tool to improve vaccination program performance in similar contexts. This conclusion is a direct, modest generalization consistent with the trial findings presented.

65.Option: Text message reminders could be combined with incentives and/or approaches to increase access to vaccination services to improve the timeliness of birth dose vaccines, as suggested by a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 88 randomized trials from 17 countries.
Evidence: Text reminders might address parental forgetfulness and enhance communication regarding vaccination appointments and will reach mobile caregivers who are unlikely to be found at home. We leveraged the widespread use of mobile phones and text reminders as a low-cost intervention to nudge parents toward timely vaccinations, ultimately increasing immunization rates.
